newsitem.title: USA: Researchers test reversing blood flow in stroke victims.
newsitem.headline: Researchers test reversing blood flow in stroke victims.

text.p: Doctors have found they can prevent brain damage in some stroke victims by rerouting blood into the brain through veins that typically transport it in the opposite direction, researchers announced on Friday.
The experimental treatment, known as neuroperfusion, is similar to a common practice of treating heart attack patients by reversing the blood flow so the organ receives oxygen.

Although the technique needs to be tested on more patients before it is reviewed for approval, it offers the potential of a breakthrough treatment for strokes, one of the most difficult medical conditions to treat.

"It's a back-door therapy," Dr. John Frazee, clinical professor of neurosurgery at the University of California at Los Angeles said. "If you think of a stroke patient as having the front door locked, you can go around the back door and still get into the house."
In most strokes, a blood clot cuts off the flow of blood to the brain, which can result in anything from mild brain damage that can be corrected with physical therapy, to paralysis, or death.

The neuroperfusion treatment is a more refined version of a procedure that has been tried without much success since the early 1900s. Frazee's team developed ways to control the speed and flow of the blood, making the treatment safer and more effective.

The technique involves pumping oxygen-rich blood out of the body through a catheter that is inserted in veins in the back of the head. While these veins are already occupied draining blood out of the brain, Frazee said it is possible to reverse the flow in a few veins, without increasing blood pressure, causing hemorrhaging or otherwise disrupting the overall flow of blood through the body.
"It's like the freeway," he said. "If the police decide they need one lane to move in the opposite direction, they can put up cones, and the cars move into the other lanes."
So far his team at the UCLA Stroke Center has tested the treatment on six patients, four of whom Frazee said had a "dramatic reversal" of their condition. The other two did not respond.
Because a disruption of oxygen to the brain can quickly cause irreversible damage, doctors have believed that not much can be done for stroke victims.

That changed somewhat last year, after the FDA approved Genentech Inc's Activase as the first stroke drug. But Activase, which dissolves blood clots, must be administered within three hours of an attack, meaning most stroke victims do not qualify.

Frazee said neuroperfusion could be applied up to seven hours after an attack, offering a new treatment to thousands of patients. Strokes are the leading cause of adult disability in the United States, affecting 400,000 people each year.
